With the team lead on leave and the quarter-end report due on Friday, the analytics floor in Kochi had split into two camps: Francis's "old team" and the new hires who sat by the window. Every lunch, someone pulled Wasim aside.
"You're with us, right?" Francis said on Tuesday, walking him to the canteen. "Those window guys say you copy their queries. Tell me what they say about me, so I know."
Wasim felt the pull. Francis's side would be safer; he had been here five years.
"I'll be honest, Francis. I'm not going to carry what anyone says," Wasim said. "Not to you, not to them."
Francis's face cooled. "Suit yourself."
That week Wasim ate lunch with the window group on Wednesday and at Francis's table on Thursday, and spent his evenings fixing the broken data pipeline everyone had avoided. When the report went out on time on Friday, the lead, back from leave, asked who had fixed the pipeline. Both camps said, "Wasim."

qa.q: When was the quarter-end report due?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: What did Wasim feel when Francis asked him to report back?
qa.a: Tempted to side with Francis, since that felt safer with Francis's five years in the team.

qa.q: How did Wasim stay out of the office politics?
qa.a: He refused to carry tales, ate lunch with both groups, and put his effort into fixing the broken pipeline.

qa.q: How did Francis react to Wasim's refusal?
qa.a: Coolly ("Suit yourself"), disappointed not to gain an ally.

grounding: Shows office groups pulling a newcomer in, and staying friendly to all, doing good work and refusing to pass tales.

In his third month at the insurance office in Gurugram, Naveen saw how things worked: Deepika's lunch group mocked the new regional manager, and the manager rewarded whoever brought him news.
On Monday Deepika said, laughing, "Rastogi sir thinks spreadsheets are a personality." Naveen laughed too. That afternoon, alone with Rastogi sir at the printer, he felt the urge to mention it, casually. It would make him look loyal. It might even get him the client visit he wanted.
He opened his mouth, then closed it. He thought about sitting next to Deepika afterwards.
Instead he said, "Sir, I've finished the claims review early. Can I take the Faridabad client visit?"
Rastogi sir looked at the report, nodded, and said yes.
At lunch the next day Deepika started another joke. Naveen smiled, said, "Let's give him a month," and changed the subject to cricket. Nobody at the table seemed to mind.

qa.q: What did Deepika say about Rastogi sir?
qa.a: "Rastogi sir thinks spreadsheets are a personality."

qa.q: Why was Naveen tempted to repeat Deepika's joke to Rastogi sir?
qa.a: He wanted to look loyal and hoped it might win him the client visit, a pull towards safety through tale-carrying.

qa.q: How did Naveen stay friendly to all without taking sides?
qa.a: He kept the joke to himself, earned the visit by finishing the review early, and gently steered the lunch table away from gossip.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel if she learned Naveen had passed on the joke?
qa.a: Betrayed and exposed, unable to trust him at the lunch table again.

grounding: Illustrates office gossip and the temptation to pass tales for safety, and choosing good work and friendliness to all instead.

passage:
For her first two weeks at the software office in Hitech City, Pallavi ate lunch at her desk. The rest of the team went down at 1 p.m. in a loud group, and nobody asked her. She decided they were a snobbish clique and started wearing earphones all day.
On Friday, standing in the pantry, she overheard Harsha say, "The new girl never talks. I think she wants to be left alone."
She almost walked out. Instead she turned around. "Hi, I'm Pallavi. I don't want to be left alone, actually. I just didn't know if I could join."
Harsha went red. "Oh! Sorry. We just go down at 1. Anyone can come."
On Monday she took off her earphones and went down at 1. She didn't say much that first day; she asked about the biryani place. On Wednesday someone asked her opinion on a new phone. By the third week, she was the one saving a seat for the next new joiner.

qa.q: At what time does the team go down for lunch?
qa.a: At 1 p.m.

qa.q: What had Pallavi assumed about the team, and how did she feel?
qa.a: That they were a snobbish clique; she felt left out and hurt, and hid behind her earphones.

qa.q: What small steps helped Pallavi join in?
qa.a: Introducing herself to Harsha, taking off her earphones, going down at 1, and starting with small conversations.

qa.q: How had Harsha seen Pallavi?
qa.a: As someone who wanted to be left alone, because she never talked.

grounding: Shows a newcomer left out of team lunches, and introducing herself and joining small conversations instead of assuming hostility.

Note from the internship coordinator, law firm placement, week 5
I visited the firm today for Dilnaz's mid-internship review. She has spent five weeks photocopying, filing and fetching lunch for the associate she reports to, Trisha. She has not been to court once or drafted a single document. In the break room, she told me quietly that she felt "useless" and too embarrassed to tell her parents what she does all day.
I suggested she request a defined role, in writing. We drafted three lines together: what she hopes to learn, one task she would like to try, and a request for fifteen minutes of feedback each Friday.
She sent it to Trisha before I left. Trisha replied within the hour, apologising: she had been swamped and had not planned for an intern. Dilnaz will attend a hearing on Tuesday and draft a notice.
If nothing changes in two weeks, I have told Dilnaz we can discuss moving her to another placement.

qa.q: How many weeks had Dilnaz spent photocopying and filing?
qa.a: Five weeks.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel about her internship?
qa.a: Useless, and too embarrassed to tell her parents what she did all day.

qa.q: What did the coordinator help Dilnaz ask for?
qa.a: A clear role in writing: what she hopes to learn, one task to try, and fifteen minutes of feedback each Friday.

qa.q: Why had Trisha given Dilnaz only menial tasks?
qa.a: She had been swamped and hadn't planned for an intern, and she apologised quickly.

grounding: Shows an intern given only menial work, and asking for a clear role and feedback, with a plan to move on if nothing changes.

"Dhruv, the client wants the dashboard by 5, and I've broken the filter again," Nandini said, spinning her chair round.
Dhruv looked at his own pile of work. It would be faster to take her laptop and fix it. Or to hand her his boring data cleaning and build the dashboard himself.
He pulled a chair over instead. "Show me what you clicked."

Afterwards she said, "You could have fixed it in one minute."

qa.a: By 5.

qa.q: What did Dhruv feel when Nandini broke the filter again?
qa.a: Pressed for time and tempted to take her laptop and fix it himself, or to hand her his boring data cleaning.

qa.q: How did Dhruv teach patiently?

qa.q: How might Nandini feel when Dhruv credits her to the client?
qa.a: Proud and seen, knowing her work was recognised in front of the client.

When Yogesh joined our lab as a summer intern, I did exactly what I'd hated as an intern: I gave him all my dull tasks. Label two hundred sample tubes. Clean the fridge. Enter old data. I told myself it was "learning the basics".
In week two I saw him in the corridor, reading a paper on his phone about the very experiment I was running. He had never asked to join. He probably thought he couldn't.
I felt ashamed. So I asked him to run the next trial with me. I explained each step slowly, let him pipette, and didn't sigh when he spilled the first plate. By week five he found an error in my calibration that I had missed for a month.
At our lab meeting I put his name on the slide: "Calibration fix: Yogesh." Our professor asked him to explain it. He did, nervously, and well.
I still give him some boring tasks. I also do some of them myself.
— Usha

qa.q: How many sample tubes did Usha ask Yogesh to label?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: How did Usha feel on seeing Yogesh read the paper in the corridor?
qa.a: Ashamed of dumping dull tasks on him, realising he wanted to learn but thought he couldn't ask.

qa.q: How did Usha change the way of mentoring Yogesh?
qa.a: By inviting him into the trial, explaining patiently, allowing mistakes, and crediting his calibration fix on the slide.

It was past 9 p.m., the office in Noida almost empty, the product launch due at midnight, when Bhupen, the senior developer, pulled a chair close to Yash's desk again. "Working late for me, handsome?" His hand settled on Yash's shoulder.
It was the fourth time this month. Yash had laughed it off before, because Bhupen reviewed his code and everyone called Bhupen "a joker".
This time Yash stood up and stepped away. "Bhupen, don't touch me, and stop the comments. I mean it."
Bhupen raised his hands. "Relax, just fun."
"It's not fun for me."
Yash went back to his screen, heart pounding, and opened a note on his phone: the date, the time, the words, and the three earlier times he could remember. At 12:10, after the launch, he emailed HR from home with the note attached.
HR replied at 9 the next morning: "Thank you for reporting this. None of this is on you. We'll meet you at 11, and from today you'll report to a different reviewer."

qa.q: How many times this month had Bhupen done this?
qa.a: It was the fourth time this month.

qa.q: Why had Yash laughed it off before?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable but afraid to object, since Bhupen reviewed his code and everyone called Bhupen a joker.

qa.q: What steps did Yash take?
qa.a: He said no clearly, stepped away, wrote down the dates, times and words, and emailed HR with the note that night.

qa.q: How does HR respond?
qa.a: The next morning it thanks Yash, says it is not his fault, sets a meeting at 11 and assigns a different reviewer.

grounding: Shows a colleague's unwanted comments and touch, saying no clearly, documenting dates and words and reporting to HR, with the message that it is not his fault.

Akash was stuck in a flooded underpass on his way in, and the regional director had arrived a day early. "Mohit, walk me through the vendor savings," she said, sitting down.
Mohit opened the deck they had built together. The best idea in it, renegotiating the transport contract, was Akash's. The director didn't know that. Akash wasn't there. And the promotion list was being drafted next month.
"I built most of this," Mohit heard himself begin. Then he stopped. It wasn't true, and he would have to look at Akash tomorrow.
He started again. "Akash and I built this together. The transport renegotiation was his idea; he made the calls. I did the numbers on the packaging side."
The director made a note. "Tell Akash I want to talk to him about the transport piece."
At noon Akash arrived, soaked. "How did it go?"
"She wants to talk to you," Mohit said. "It was your idea."

qa.q: Why did Mohit begin with "I built most of this"?

qa.q: What made Mohit change course, and why was it right?

qa.q: How might Akash feel when Mohit says "It was your idea"?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, and more trusting of Mohit.

At the agency in Lower Parel, the campaign line that won the pitch, "Small steps, big city", had come out of a late-night chat between Samir and Baljeet. When the creative head asked at the celebration meeting, "Whose line was that?", Samir said, "Mine," and everyone clapped.

Baljeet said nothing. But for two weeks he stopped staying late, stopped sending sketches after hours, and ate lunch with the design team instead.

qa.a: "Small steps, big city".

qa.q: How did Samir feel after taking the credit, and how did he justify it?
qa.a: He rationalised that Baljeet was a designer and the phrasing was mostly his; underneath, he felt uneasy, noticing the change "like a draught".

qa.q: How did Samir repair the damage?
qa.a: He told the creative head the line was Baljeet's and apologised to Baljeet directly, without excuses.

qa.q: How did Baljeet respond to losing the credit?
qa.a: He quietly withdrew, no longer staying late or sending sketches, and ate lunch with the design team.

At the milk-collection centre in Anand district, forty litres had gone sour overnight. When the supervisor, Patel-kaka, asked who had closed the chiller, Mehak said quickly, "Sahil was last out."
Sahil felt heat climb his neck. He had left at six; Mehak had stayed till eight to count the evening cans. He knew about her unpaid tea-stall tab too, and her late mornings. It would be easy to fling all of it back.

Mehak looked at the floor. "I thought I'd set it right."
"It happens," Sahil said quietly. "Maybe we both sign the temperature from now on?"
Patel-kaka nodded and wrote a new rule on the board: two signatures at closing. At the gate later, Mehak said, "Sorry." He nodded. That was enough.

qa.a: Angry, with heat climbing his neck, and tempted to throw her other slips back at her.

In today's check-in it was clear that Maria has written most of the group's field report. The shared document's history shows her edits on eleven of fourteen pages. Hansa, assigned the interview section, has added two paragraphs in three weeks.

passage:
Tanuja,
I've been meaning to write since the presentation on Friday.
When Professor Das praised the survey design, I said, "Thank you, we worked hard on that." Everyone looked at me, and I kept going as if it was mine. It wasn't. You designed the survey and ran the pilot. I skipped two of our meetings and mostly formatted slides.
I told myself it didn't matter who said thank you. It did. I saw your face.
I've emailed Professor Das to say the survey was your work, and I've copied you in. For the final report, I'll write the literature review and the appendix, the parts I left to you, and send drafts by Wednesday so you can check them.
I'm sorry. I relied on you to cover for me and then took the credit. I won't do that again.
Kunal

qa.q: What did Professor Das praise?
qa.a: The survey design.

qa.q: How does Kunal feel about the presentation?
qa.a: Ashamed and guilty, having accepted credit after doing little.

qa.q: What does Kunal do to make it right?
qa.a: Emails Professor Das to credit Tanuja, and takes on the literature review and appendix with drafts by Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt at the presentation?
qa.a: Hurt and overlooked, watching Kunal accept praise for Tanuja's work.

grounding: Illustrates free-riding on a groupmate and then claiming credit at the presentation, followed by owning it and contributing honestly.
